title: DELIVERY OF MANGROL – THE THIRD ANTI-SUBMARINE WARFARE SHALLOW WATER CRAFT BUILT BY CSL, KOCHI
body_text:
‘Mangrol’ , the third Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft built by Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL), Kochi, was delivered to Indian Navy on 21 Aug 2026.
The ship comprises of over 80 percent indigenous content and is equipped for underwater surveillance, Anti-Submarine Warfare (ASW) operations in coastal waters, Low -Intensity Maritime Operations (LIMO), along with mine warfare capabilities . The ship is propelled by waterjets and equipped with state -of-the-art Torpedoes , Anti-Submarine rockets, along with advanced radars and sonars.
Mangrol derives its name from the coastal town and minor port of ‘Mangrol’, located in Junagadh district of Gujarat, which is a prominent harbour for the marine fishing industry. The ship also encapsulates the legacy of erstwhile INS Mangrol, an Indian Naval Minesweeper which remained in service till 2004, thereby continuing the naval tradition of preserving distinguished warship names.
The delivery of Mangrol is yet another milestone in the Indian Navy’s indigenous shipbuilding journey and a reaffirmation of the Government’s vision of ‘ Aatmanirbhar Bharat ’ . The ship stands as a testament to the growing strength of the indigenous defence manufacturing ecosystem.

enrichment.summary: The Indian Navy received 'Mangrol', the third Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft (ASW-SWC) built by Cochin Shipyard Limited, on 21 August 2026. The vessel is over 80% indigenous, waterjet-propelled, and equipped with torpedoes, anti-submarine rockets, radars and sonars for coastal ASW, mine warfare and low-intensity maritime operations. It is named after the port town of Mangrol in Gujarat's Junagadh district, reviving the name of a former INS Mangrol minesweeper retired in 2004.
enrichment.context:
The ASW Shallow Water Craft (ASW-SWC) project is a series of eight vessels being built by CSL for the Indian Navy to replace ageing Abhay-class corvettes, aimed at strengthening coastal anti-submarine and mine countermeasure capabilities against increasing submarine activity in the Indian Ocean Region. These platforms are smaller, more agile vessels designed for littoral and shallow-water operations where larger frigates and destroyers are less effective. The naming convention after Indian coastal towns and ports (like Mangrol) also reflects the Navy's practice of honouring maritime heritage and local geography.

This delivery fits within India's broader push for defence indigenisation under 'Aatmanirbhar Bharat', with the Ministry of Defence setting targets for domestic content in naval shipbuilding and promoting public sector yards like CSL, Mazagon Dock, and Garden Reach Shipbuilders as anchors of the indigenous defence-industrial ecosystem. Such deliveries, while incremental, are part of a larger narrative of reducing import dependence in defence production and building indigenous design and manufacturing capacity in shipbuilding.
